briefing.summary: Dive on the summit of Kama'ehuakanaloa, the youngest and only fully submarine volcano in the Hawaiian chain, then scan the low-temperature, iron-rich hydrothermal vents inside Pele's Pit -- the crater left by the volcano's 1996 summit collapse. Optional objectives trace the south rift zone, the volcano's most active flank.
facts: Renamed from Lo'ihi to Kama'ehuakanaloa in July 2021 by the Hawai'i Board on Geographic Names, restoring a name drawn from Hawaiian mele recorded decades before the 1955 descriptive name.
The summit sits under roughly 975-1,000 m of water; the volcano rises more than 3,000 m from the surrounding seafloor and could breach the surface as a new Hawaiian island in 10,000-100,000 years.
A July-August 1996 earthquake swarm -- the largest ever recorded at any Hawaiian volcano -- collapsed the old summit hydrothermal site, forming the ~600 m-wide, ~300 m-deep Pele's Pit.
Vent fluids here are low in sulfide and rich in dissolved iron, feeding iron-oxidizing microbial mats instead of the black-smoker chimneys found at sulfide-rich vent fields.
hazards: This is an active volcano: seismic swarms and eruptions have reshaped the summit before (1996) and could again.
Vent fluids run warm (20-50 degC) rather than scalding, but stay clear of active orifices.
Steep local relief around Pele's Pit and the south rift; watch altitude near the vent sites.

objectives.title: Survey the Hiolo North vent site
objectives.hint: The Hiolo North vent site lies southwest of the summit inside Pele's Pit, around 1,300 m.

objectives.title: Survey the Hiolo South vent site
objectives.hint: The Hiolo South vent site lies south of the summit inside Pele's Pit, around 1,275 m.

objectives.title: Trace the south rift zone
objectives.hint: Trace the south rift zone south from the summit through the deepening volcanic slope, around 1,280 m here.
